scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

Consider: - **Betrayal:** He likely saw you as his heir, someone who’d honor his legacy. Your action feels like a **personal attack** on his competence and worth. - **Generational Conflict:** You’re right that you’re opposites, but **his pain isn’t about "action vs. ideas"**—it’s about **being replaced**. Your dad may feel his **role as provider/mentor is being undermined**. - **Face and honor** are critical. Publicly "stealing" from him (even if you’re the executor) is a **deep insult** in cultural terms. --- ### **3. His idea is now your success, and he deserves a stake. #### **C. Apologize to Your Sister and Mom** - Your mom’s support may be conditional on your dad’s feelings. **Don’t assume she’ll always side with you**—her loyalty is to the family’s harmony. - Your sister is caught in the middle. **Don’t dismiss her feelings**—she likely feels torn between you and her dad. #### **D. Accept the Consequences** - If your dad refuses to reconcile, **respect his boundaries**. You can’t force him to accept you back. - **Family relationships are irreversible.** You may never fully repair this, but you can **own your mistake** and move forward with integrity. --- ### **4. Long-Term Reflection: What Does This Say About You?** This situation reveals: - **Your strengths:** Drive, ambition, and execution. - **Your flaws:** Lack of empathy, poor judgment in family dynamics, and a **culture of entitlement** ("I’m the man of action, so I deserve this"). - **The cost:** You’ve gained financial success but **lost trust, respect, and possibly your dad’s love**. **Question for you:** If your dad had done the same to *your* idea, how would you feel? Would you accept 20% and call it fair? Or would you demand justice? --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **0 (Wrong).** - You violated trust, exploited a vulnerable family member, and built success on his back. - Your dad’s anger isn’t overblown—it’s a **justified reaction to betrayal**. - While you’ve achieved success, **you’ve paid a moral price** that may haunt you (or your relationship) for years. --- ### **What You Can Do Now:** 1. **Write a heartfelt letter** to your dad (even if you don’t send it). Acknowledge his pain, take full responsibility, and propose a fair resolution. 2. **Consult a family therapist** (if possible) to navigate this conflict with professional guidance. 3. **Decide if this is the legacy you want.** If you’re okay with being seen as a "family traitor," that’s your choice—but don’t pretend it’s morally neutral. --- ### **A Final Thought:** Your grandad was right about one thing: **you’re more like him in temperament**.
